issues.legal_issue: A co-owner acquires title by adverse possession when exclusive possession is openly hostile to the other co-owners, who know of the hostile claim, and continues for the applicable limitation period.
material_facts: The parties were co-owners, but the plaintiff had exclusively possessed the disputed land for a long time, with revenue records showing his exclusive possession.
The plaintiff asserted ownership hostile to the other co-owners, including in a written statement in an earlier suit; the other co-owners knew of that assertion.
The other co-owners had filed partition suits, which were dismissed, and the plaintiff continued in exclusive possession.
The present suit was filed more than twelve years after the hostile claim was at least clearly made in the earlier suit.
The courts below found, after considering the evidence and the parties’ conduct, that the plaintiff had established hostile possession and ouster.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the plaintiff had acquired title by ousting the other co-owners, and found no legal infirmity in the concurrent findings. The judgment’s final sentence nevertheless states that the appeal is allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 64 and 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the person asserting adverse possession bears the burden of proving it; possession by one co-owner is presumed to be on behalf of all unless the contrary is proved. Adverse possession requires open, hostile possession, denial of the true owners’ rights, animus possidendi, and the owners’ knowledge. The Court relied on Saroop Singh v. Banto, Govindammal v. R. Perumal Chettiar, and T. Anjanappa v. Somalingappa for the burden and requirements of adverse possession.

rule.if: appeal_from_concurrent_findings and co_ownership and exclusive_possession and hostile_ownership_claim and other_owners_knew and limitation_period_elapsed

predicates.appeal_from_concurrent_findings: The case is an appeal challenging concurrent findings in a suit concerning title by adverse possession.
predicates.co_ownership: The parties held the property as co-owners.
predicates.exclusive_possession: One co-owner possessed and enjoyed the disputed property exclusively rather than on behalf of the other co-owners.
predicates.hostile_ownership_claim: The possessor openly asserted ownership in denial of the other co-owners’ title.
predicates.other_owners_knew: The other co-owners knew of the possessor’s hostile claim and exclusive possession.
predicates.limitation_period_elapsed: The hostile possession continued for longer than the applicable limitation period.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges concurrent findings in a co-ownership dispute, exclusive possession coupled with a known hostile ownership claim lasting beyond the applicable limitation period results in acquired title by adverse possession.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to use the specific term ouster in a plaint does not defeat a claim where the pleadings, read as a whole, state the necessary facts and the parties understood the case they had to meet.
material_facts: The plaint alleged that the plaintiff had possessed the disputed land as owner and adversely to the defendants for twelve years.
The plaint did not specifically use the term ouster.
The parties went to trial knowing their respective cases, and the defendants were not misled or prevented from presenting evidence.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the pleadings were sufficient despite the absence of a specific plea using the terminology of ouster.
issues.legal_principle: Pleadings must be construed reasonably and as a whole, and pleadings in mofussil courts are to be construed liberally. The Court relied on Devasahayam (D) by LRs. v. P. Savithramma and Ors. and held that omission of the appropriate terminology does not itself mean the statutory ingredients are absent.

rule.if: mofussil_proceeding and pleadings_state_hostile_exclusive_possession and parties_understood_the_case and no_trial_prejudice

predicates.mofussil_proceeding: The claim was brought in a mofussil court.
predicates.pleadings_state_hostile_exclusive_posses: The pleadings, read as a whole, allege possession as owner in denial of the other owners’ rights.
predicates.parties_understood_the_case: The parties understood the factual case each side was advancing.
predicates.no_trial_prejudice: The omission did not mislead a party or prevent that party from presenting evidence.

issues.definition: In a mofussil proceeding, a pleading that states hostile exclusive possession is not defeated by omitting the word ouster when the parties understood the case and the omission caused no trial prejudice.

issues.legal_issue: Pendency of a partition suit does not stop limitation from running against a person in continuing hostile possession.
material_facts: The other co-owners filed suits seeking partition and separate possession, and those suits were dismissed.
The plaintiff continued to possess the disputed land exclusively while asserting hostile ownership to the other co-owners’ knowledge.
The present suit was filed after the hostile possession had continued for more than the applicable limitation period.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the pending partition suits did not stop limitation from running, and that the limitation period could run at least from the plaintiff’s hostile declaration in the earlier suit.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that pendency of a suit does not stop the running of limitation. It applied Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, to the claim of title by adverse possession.

predicates.adverse_possession_claim: A party claims title through adverse possession.
predicates.prior_partition_suit_pending: A partition suit concerning the property is pending between the parties.
predicates.hostile_possession_continued: The claimant continues exclusive possession while openly denying the other owners’ title.

issues.definition: When a partition suit is pending, its pendency does not stop limitation from running if the adverse-possession claimant continues exclusive possession while openly denying the other owners’ title.
